MS_R05_PROPOSITION: INTRO-U001: Motivation: observable but under-explained cross-project Reference evidence in OSS DBMS ecosystems; DBMS projects form long-lived collaborative ecosystems; DBMS is a meaningful vertical setting without presupposing it differs from all other OSS
EN_R02_PROPOSITION: INTRO-P001:  ## 1 Introduction  ### 1.1 Observable Reference Evidence in the Open-Source DBMS Ecosystem  Open-source database management system (DBMS) ecosystems leave observable cross-project Reference evidence whose project-level meaning has not yet been adequately explained. Open-source DBMS projects such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MongoDB, Redis, ClickHouse, and TiDB serve a large number of downstream applications, and they have also formed continuously evolving collaborative ecosystems around kernel implementation, storage mechanisms, query execution, extension interfaces, and operational tooling. Long-term maintenance, compatibility constraints, extension mechanisms, and links to standards, drivers, tools, and test resources make DBMS a meaningful vertical setting for examining explicit Reference evidence and project-level structural relations, without presupposing that DBMS projects differ from all other OSS projects. (Throughout the paper, capitalized *Reference* denotes the explicit-reference relation type defined in §3.3.1.)

EN_R02_PROPOSITION: INTRO-P002A:  From a software-ecosystem perspective, open-source research has broadened from single-project quality, contributor participation, and code evolution to cross-project dependencies, ecosystem governance, knowledge diffusion, and socio-technical coordination [@francobedoya2017ossecosystems; @manikas2013ecosystemslr; @manikas2016revisitingecosystems]. Within the DBMS setting, prior studies have examined DBMS extensibility and DBMS adoption in open-source projects, showing that extension mechanisms, system adaptation, and adoption contexts can be studied as domain problems in their own right [@kim2025dbmsextensibility; @paiva2025dbmsadoption]. Other empirical work has documented the use of multiple database models in open-source projects and the joint evolution of source code and schemas in FOSS projects [@benats2021multidatabasemodels; @vassiliadis2023sourceschemaevolution]. These established domain phenomena, together with the cross-project toolchain context of DBMS and technical concerns such as SQL dialects, transactions, replication, storage, and query processing, motivate DBMS as an empirical setting for examining collaboration contexts, explicit Reference targets, and inter-project structural relations. We do not read these studies as evidence for all collaboration or Reference motives. || INTRO-P002B:  This evidence originates in collaboration records. When maintainers reference other projects, standards documents, test cases, code implementations, or earlier discussions in issues, pull requests, commits, and comments, they can leave traceable evidence of problem localization, solution comparison, dependency notes, or added context. In DBMS projects, references to external specifications, performance benchmarks, compatibility issues, and other implementations make the setting a domain-specific empirical environment for examining such cross-project evidence. Building project-level relations from these collaboration traces therefore requires preserving the direction, project membership, and aggregated strength of the Reference evidence, together with the conditions under which it can be interpreted.

EN_R02_PROPOSITION: THREAT-P004:  ### 6.2 Internal Validity  Threats to internal validity arise mainly from Reference extraction, entity validation, membership mapping and repository resolution, and quotient construction. GitHub Docs describe the platform syntax and linking mechanisms of autolinked references and PR–issue linking [@githubdocs2026autolinked; @githubdocs2026linkingprissue], and IREL provides a rule framework for identifying references between GitHub projects [@liu2022irel]. On this basis, the GH_CoRE processing chain uses rules, regular-expression patterns, and the GitHub API to validate accessible objects. Rule-based extraction may still miss version numbers, short hashes, URL variants, dead links, or implicit references in natural language, and it may include ambiguous matches. We report these as limitations of our method, not as empirical false-positive or false-negative rates derived from the platform documentation. Errors in fine-grained entity typing and repository membership resolution propagate into RefQ relations, and automated events may amplify some Reference types. Finally, membership-induced aggregation makes project-level structure more analyzable at the cost of specific artifact semantics.

EN_R02_PROPOSITION: THREAT-P008:  **Observation / network-boundary validity.** The RefQN is a seed-centered observed quotient network: under the observation contract, the 294 seed projects are source-complete, whereas expanded target projects are source-incomplete. MS_R05_PROPOSITION: ABS-U001: Abstract: cross-project explicit references beyond package/code dependency; lifting them to traceable project-level relations needs membership, aggregation and observation semantics; RefQ aggregates directed fine-grained references via artifact-to-project membership into weighted directed RefQN; 294 seeds; IssueComment main source carrier, external links main target; heterogeneous source scope and target coverage; first-order undirected view broadly connected but Louvain seed-sensitive; subdomain differences only in some role/local-structure metrics and vary with label handling; RefQ gives traceable project-level structural representation
EN_R02_PROPOSITION: ABS-P001:  ## Abstract  Explicit references in open-source software projects can record cross-project associations that lie beyond package dependencies and code calls. Lifting such fine-grained collaborative references to interpretable and traceable project-level relations, however, requires explicit semantics for project membership, aggregation, and observation. We introduce the Reference Quotient (RefQ), which aggregates fine-grained directed Reference relations into a weighted, directed, project-level Reference Quotient Network (RefQN) on the basis of artifact-to-project semantic membership. Using 294 open-source DBMS projects as source-side seeds, we analyze the composition of Reference evidence, project-level source and target roles, first-order undirected structural characteristics, and subdomain differences; because source behavior is observed completely for the seeds but not for the expanded targets they reference, source roles, target roles, and the direction-ignored view are interpreted separately. Results show that IssueComment is the main referencing carrier and that GitHub service and external links form the largest referenced-entity category. Projects differ markedly in their outgoing Reference scope and in the coverage they receive as targets. The first-order undirected view of the seed-centered observed RefQN is broadly connected, but its Louvain partition is sensitive to the random seed. Subdomain differences appear mainly in some network-role and local-structure metrics and vary with label handling. In the studied open-source DBMS setting, RefQ provides a traceable project-level structural representation of explicit references and can be used to characterize cross-project Reference roles and the organization of the resulting network.
